title: A 2,000-year-old Greek device predicted eclipses with at least 30 bronze gears

cover.alt: The corroded, greenish bronze fragments of the Antikythera mechanism, with gear teeth visible, displayed at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

body: In 1901 sponge divers pulled a corroded lump of bronze from a Roman-era shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, 45 m down. A year later someone noticed a gear wheel inside it. X-rays and CT scans have since revealed **at least 30 interlocking gears** that modelled the Sun and Moon moving through the zodiac, the Moon’s phases and the timing of eclipses, using cycles such as the 223-month Saros. It was probably built in the 2nd century BC, and nothing of similar complexity is known again until the astronomical clocks of 14th-century Europe.

slides.alt: A modern reconstruction of the Antikythera mechanism in a wooden case, showing a large front dial with concentric rings and pointers.
slides.caption: A modern model of the front dial. The original case was roughly 34 by 18 by 9 cm, though its exact size is uncertain.

slides.question: How many separate fragments of the mechanism are known today?
slides.explanation: 82 fragments, of which only four contain gears. Many of the others carry inscriptions, a kind of user’s guide that CT scans finally made readable in 2005.

slides.heading: Only 4 of the 82 known fragments contain gears
slides.note: Seven fragments are mechanically significant; most of the rest are covered in tiny inscriptions.

slides.heading: What it could do
slides.text: Turn the mechanism and its pointers moved: the Sun and Moon through the zodiac, the Moon’s phase, and dials that predicted eclipses with the 223-month Saros cycle and tracked the 19-year Metonic cycle of 235 months. Another dial counted down to the four-yearly cycle of the Panhellenic games.

slides.question: Where was the mechanism found?
slides.explanation: Sponge divers found it in 1901 in a wreck off Antikythera, in about 45 m of water. The ship itself went down around 70–60 BC.

slides.heading: A long gap
slides.text: Machines of similar complexity did not appear again until the 14th century in western Europe, with the first astronomical clocks. Whether the mechanism also showed the five planets known to the Greeks is uncertain: no planetary gearing survives, though inscriptions mention the cycles of Venus and Saturn.
